title: How do you implement per-user rate limiting in a distributed environment (Redis + token/leaky bucket, Bucket4j, gateway)?
shortTitle: How do you implement per-user rate limiting in a distributed environment

s1_definition.profdef: Per-user rate limiting in a distributed environment means enforcing a request quota for each individual user consistently across all service instances, which requires a shared, atomic counter rather than per-instance local state. The standard approach is to key the limit by user or API key and store the counter in a shared store like Redis, updating it atomically — often with a Lua script or a library like Bucket4j backed by Redis — so that no matter which instance a request lands on, all instances see and decrement the same bucket. The enforcement typically lives at the API gateway so excess requests are rejected with HTTP 429 before reaching the backends.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India lets each customer submit at most ten forms per minute, but the bank has five branches and a customer might walk into any of them. If each branch kept its own private tally, the customer could submit ten forms at every branch and sneak through fifty, defeating the rule. So instead the bank keeps one central ledger, shared by all branches, that records how many forms each customer has submitted this minute. Every branch checks and updates that one central ledger before accepting a form. Now it does not matter which branch the customer visits; the limit of ten per minute is enforced across the whole bank as a single truth. That central shared ledger is Redis, and checking it before admitting a request is distributed per-user rate limiting.
s1_definition.oneliner: Distributed per-user rate limiting keeps one shared, atomic counter per user in Redis so the quota is enforced across every instance, usually at the gateway, rejecting excess with 429.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Per-user rate limiting in a distributed environment means enforcing a request quota for each individual user consistently across all service instances, which requires a shared, atomic counter rather than per-instance local state. The standard approach is to key the limit by user or API key and store the counter in a shared store like Redis, updating it atomically — often with a Lua script or a library like Bucket4j backed by Redis — so that no matter which instance a request lands on, all instances see and decrement the same bucket. The enforcement typically lives at the API gateway so excess requests are rejected with HTTP 429 before reaching the backends.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India lets each customer submit at most ten forms per minute, but the bank has five branches and a customer might walk into any of them. If each branch kept its own private tally, the customer could submit ten forms at every branch and sneak through fifty, defeating the rule. So instead the bank keeps one central ledger, shared by all branches, that records how many forms each customer has submitted this minute. Every branch checks and updates that one central ledger before accepting a form. Now it does not matter which branch the customer visits; the limit of ten per minute is enforced across the whole bank as a single truth. That central shared ledger is Redis, and checking it before admitting a request is distributed per-user rate limiting.

**One line to remember:** Distributed per-user rate limiting keeps one shared, atomic counter per user in Redis so the quota is enforced across every instance, usually at the gateway, rejecting excess with 429.

sections.s2_technical:
The core problem is that a naive rate limiter stores its counters in the memory of a single instance, which breaks the moment you run more than one instance. If the per-user limit is one hundred requests per minute and you run five instances behind a load balancer, each instance independently allows one hundred, so the user effectively gets five hundred. To enforce the limit for the whole system, the counter must be shared and updated atomically, and the natural home for that shared counter is a fast in-memory store like Redis that every instance can reach.

The counter is keyed by the identity you want to limit, which for per-user limiting is the user id or API key, often combined with the route and the time window, for example a key like `rate:user:SAV2001:transfers`. Each request increments or decrements this shared value, and the update must be atomic so that concurrent requests from different instances cannot both read a stale value and overshoot the limit. Redis provides this atomicity through single commands like INCR with EXPIRE, or more precisely through a Lua script that reads, checks, and updates in one indivisible server-side operation, which is how robust implementations avoid race conditions.

The algorithm chosen shapes behavior. A token bucket, implemented in Redis, stores the current token count and a last-refill timestamp per user; each request runs a script that refills tokens based on elapsed time, and if at least one token remains it consumes one and allows the request, otherwise it rejects. This permits controlled bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a steady long-run rate. A leaky bucket instead enforces a constant outflow, smoothing bursts into a steady stream. A sliding-window counter blends the current and previous window counts in Redis to smooth the boundary burst that a plain fixed window would allow. The choice depends on whether you want to permit bursts (token bucket) or strictly smooth traffic (leaky bucket).

Bucket4j is the common Java library for this. It implements the token-bucket algorithm and integrates with a distributed backend through the JCache interface, so you back it with Redis (via Redisson or Infinispan) and get per-user buckets that are consistent across instances. You define a bandwidth such as one hundred tokens refilled per minute, resolve a bucket per user key, and call `tryConsume` on each request; because the bucket state lives in the shared backend, every instance consumes from the same bucket. For example, `bucket.tryConsume(1)` returns false when the user's shared bucket is empty, and you translate that into a 429.

The enforcement point matters. The cleanest place for per-user rate limiting is the API gateway, because it is the single entry point and can reject excess requests before they consume any backend capacity. Spring Cloud Gateway has a built-in Redis-backed RequestRateLimiter filter where you supply a key resolver that extracts the user id, and it runs a token-bucket script in Redis per user. Kong, Nginx, and cloud API gateways offer equivalent features. Placing it at the gateway also centralizes the policy and keeps the backend services simpler. The senior-level nuances are that you should return a 429 with a Retry-After header and ideally rate-limit headers so clients can back off gracefully, that the Redis operation must be atomic to be correct under concurrency, that Redis itself must be made highly available since it is now on the critical path, and that you often layer limits, for example a per-user limit plus a stricter per-endpoint limit for expensive operations, and sometimes fail open or fall back to a conservative local limit if Redis is briefly unavailable so that a limiter outage does not take down the whole API.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India wants to limit each user to a fixed number of transfer requests per minute to prevent abuse, and it runs several gateway instances.

Problem 1 — the first implementation kept a per-instance counter in local memory, and because there were three gateway instances, each user effectively got three times the intended limit, so a scripted client still overwhelmed the transfer service. This is exactly why the counter must be shared: a single source of truth in Redis enforces one limit across all instances.

Problem 2 — a quick fix used a plain read-then-write against Redis, but under concurrency two instances read the same remaining count and both allowed a request, overshooting the limit. This is exactly why the update must be atomic, using an indivisible Redis operation so concurrent requests cannot both consume the last token.

Problem 3 — the bank wanted to allow a small legitimate burst (a user making a few quick transfers) while still enforcing a steady average, and a fixed window allowed an unfair double burst at the boundary. This is exactly why a token bucket is a good fit: it permits a controlled burst up to the bucket size while refilling at a steady rate.

The mini-project builds a `RedisRateStore` abstraction (simulated with an atomic in-memory map standing in for Redis) that performs an atomic token-bucket check, a `DistributedRateLimiter` keyed per user, and a `GatewayInstance` that uses it so multiple simulated instances share the same store. The demo runs several gateway instances handling requests for the same user, shows the shared bucket enforcing one limit across all of them, shows the atomic consume preventing overshoot, and shows a controlled burst followed by 429s.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a shared token-bucket store refilling five tokens per second with a capacity of ten, three gateway instances all pointing at that one store, and user Rajesh firing fifteen rapid transfer requests spread across the instances.

Step 1: Rajesh's first request lands on gateway instance gw-1. The limiter builds the key for user SAV2001 on the transfers route and calls the shared store's atomic consume. The bucket starts full at ten, so a token is consumed and the request is admitted.

Step 2: The second request lands on gw-2, a different instance. Crucially, gw-2 consults the same shared bucket, not a private one, so it sees nine tokens remaining and consumes one down to eight. This is the whole point: the instances share a single source of truth.

Step 3: Requests three through ten scatter across gw-1, gw-2, and gw-3 in rotation, and each atomically consumes one token from the same shared bucket. By the tenth request the bucket is drained to zero. All ten were admitted as a controlled burst up to the capacity.

Step 4: The eleventh request lands on some instance and calls consume, but the shared bucket is empty and the refill of five per second has not yet added a whole token in the tiny elapsed time, so consume returns false and the request is rejected with a 429.

Step 5: Requests twelve through fifteen likewise find the shared bucket empty and are rejected. The atomic consume guarantees that even though different instances handled requests nearly simultaneously, no two of them both grabbed the last token, so the count never overshoots the limit.

Step 6: The totals show exactly ten admitted and five blocked. The decisive observation is that the limit enforced is ten in total, not thirty, even though three instances handled the traffic, because they all drew from the one shared Redis bucket. If each instance had kept a local counter, Rajesh would have slipped through up to thirty.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Rajesh: 15 rapid transfers across 3 gateway instances ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 WARNING 429 for user rajesh-SAV2001 on transfers (shared bucket empty across ALL instances)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Rajesh across all instances: admitted=10 (burst cap 10), blocked(429)=5
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    KEY POINT: limit enforced GLOBALLY (10), not 3x (30) — shared Redis bucket
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Remaining tokens in shared bucket: 0.0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Per-user rate limiting in a distributed environment comes down to one central idea: the counter must be shared and updated atomically, because a limiter that keeps its state in a single instance's memory breaks the moment you run more than one instance. If the limit is a hundred requests per minute per user and you run five instances behind a load balancer, each instance independently allows a hundred and the user effectively gets five hundred. So I key the limit by the user id or API key, usually combined with the route, and I store that counter in a fast shared store like Redis that every instance can reach, so there is a single source of truth.

The update has to be atomic, and this is a subtle but critical point. A naive read-then-write against Redis has a race: two instances can both read the same remaining count and both allow a request, overshooting the limit. The correct approach is an indivisible operation, either a single Redis command or, better, a Lua script that reads, refills, checks, and consumes in one server-side step, so concurrent requests from different instances can never both grab the last token. On the algorithm, I usually use a token bucket stored in Redis, which keeps the token count and a last-refill timestamp per user, refills by elapsed time, and consumes a token per request, because it permits a controlled burst up to the bucket size while enforcing a steady long-run rate. A leaky bucket is the choice when I want to strictly smooth traffic into a constant outflow, and a sliding-window counter smooths the boundary burst that a plain fixed window allows.

In Java the standard library for this is Bucket4j, which implements the token-bucket algorithm and plugs into a distributed backend through JCache, so I back it with Redis via Redisson and get per-user buckets that are consistent across instances; each request calls tryConsume on the user's bucket and I translate a false into a 429. For enforcement point, I put the limiter at the API gateway because it is the single entry point and can reject excess before it consumes any backend capacity. Spring Cloud Gateway has a built-in Redis-backed RequestRateLimiter with a key resolver that extracts the user id and runs a token-bucket script in Redis per user, and Kong and cloud gateways offer the same.

We actually walked through these mistakes on our transfer API. We first kept a per-instance counter and three gateway instances meant each user got triple the intended limit, so a scripted client still overwhelmed us. Moving the counter to Redis fixed the global enforcement. Then a plain read-then-write let two instances overshoot under load, which we fixed with an atomic Lua consume. And we chose a token bucket so a legitimate user could make a small quick burst of transfers while still being held to a steady average.

The nuances I always mention to show depth are that I return a 429 with a Retry-After header and rate-limit headers so clients back off gracefully, that Redis is now on the critical path so it must be highly available, that I often layer a per-user limit with a stricter per-endpoint limit for expensive operations, and that I design a sensible fallback, often failing open or dropping to a conservative local limit, if Redis is briefly unavailable so that a limiter hiccup does not take down the whole API. The one-line summary I leave with the interviewer is: key by user, store the bucket in Redis, consume atomically, enforce at the gateway, and the limit holds globally across every instance.

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling: add more instances behind load balancer
Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
